items.title: Plant Maintenance
items.context: Plant Maintenance

cards.title: What the Plant Maintenance module covers
cards.body:
Plant Maintenance manages the company's equipment, functional locations and vehicles, and the work done to keep them running.
It covers maintenance requests, planned and preventive schedules, maintenance orders, safety permits, meter readings, tyres, incidents and customer service under contract.
Spares for maintenance are drawn from Material Management stores.

cards.title: Who works in Plant Maintenance and what they own
cards.body:
Maintenance planners own the equipment register, schedules and maintenance orders, and supervisors and technicians report the work.
Operators and drivers record meter readings, trip sheets and fuel, while fleet staff manage tyres and incidents.
Service coordinators handle customer service calls, service orders, contracts and invoices, and safety officers issue clearance permits.

cards.title: Why the equipment and location register comes first
cards.body:
Every maintenance transaction points at a piece of equipment or a functional location, so these must be registered first with codes, hierarchy, custodian and location.
Equipment carries its spare parts list, measurement parameters, supplemental details and, for vehicles, driver and tyre layout.
Permit templates, category task lists and shutdown work lists then give planners standard content to reuse.
Changes to location, owner, driver or custody are made through controlled documents, so the register keeps a complete history.

cards.title: Common document lifecycle in Plant Maintenance
cards.body:
Most maintenance documents move through Initial, Release and Authorized, with each step stamping the user and time.
Many have their real effect only on authorisation: equipment moves, tyre status changes, schedule status changes and meter readings are applied then.
Authorised documents are locked, and changes go through an amendment or a status change document.
Only one pending document per equipment is usually allowed for location changes, replacements and meter resets, so conflicting changes cannot pile up.

cards.title: How a maintenance need flows from request to closing
cards.body:
A need arrives as a maintenance request, a work log observation, or a schedule occurrence generated when a time or meter trigger falls due.
The planner raises a maintenance order on the asset, consuming the request faults or occurrences so each need is handled once, and loads standard tasks, resources and spares.
Hazardous work needs a clearance permit, spares are issued from stores against the order, and progress is reported shift by shift.
The closing records actual times, delays, root causes and readings, and order status rolls back to the request and schedule.
Downtime, meter readings and costs from this cycle then feed availability analysis and the next round of planning.

items.title: Maintenance Master Data Setup
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Master Data Setup

cards.title: Purpose of maintenance master data setup
cards.body:
This flow registers equipment and functional locations and defines the standard content maintenance reuses: permit templates, category task lists and shutdown work lists.
Maintenance planners set it up before requests, schedules and orders are raised.
Every job then starts from a known asset and an agreed standard.

cards.title: Setup order for maintenance master data
cards.body:
Functional locations are defined first as the places in the plant, with their hierarchy and custodian.
Equipment is then registered, placed at a location and given spare parts, measurement parameters and supplemental details.
Permit templates define safety conditions for hazardous work, category task lists define standard tasks per maintenance category, and shutdown work lists define the plan for a shutdown.
Each equipment can be on only one active task list and one shutdown list, which keeps standards unambiguous.

items.title: Equipment and Asset Register Changes
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes

cards.title: Purpose of controlled equipment register changes
cards.body:
This flow changes the equipment register through controlled documents: relocation, change of owner or driver, statutory documents, downtime and replacement.
Maintenance planners and fleet administrators use it whenever equipment facts change after registration.
The register stays current and every change keeps a history.

cards.title: How register changes are controlled
cards.body:
Location and owner changes take effect only on authorisation and write history.
An equipment cannot be on two pending location changes or replacements at once.
Replacement starts with an approved request, often from a maintenance order, and is completed by a replacement document once the new equipment is installed.
Down periods record planned shutdowns or breakdowns and take their actual dates from maintenance order closings, while document entries track expiry of certificates and permits.

items.title: Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing

cards.title: Purpose of the maintenance request and order flow
cards.body:
This flow turns a reported need into a planned, permitted, executed and closed maintenance job.
Operators and supervisors raise requests, planners create orders, safety officers issue permits, and technicians report the work.
Every job is traceable from the original fault to its root cause and actual effort.

cards.title: Steps from request to closed order
cards.body:
Work logs record shift observations, and a maintenance request records the fault or service needed with priority and target date.
The planner raises a maintenance order from the request, a schedule or directly, with tasks, resources, tools and spares, and amends it if the plan changes.
A clearance permit is issued before hazardous work, and progress is reported per shift.
The closing records actual times, delays, root causes and check point results, and locks the order.

cards.title: How status flows between requests, orders and closings
cards.body:
Each request fault can be taken into only one order; saving the order marks the fault as taken and recalculates the request status.
Request status can also be changed fault by fault through a status change document, and the request follows its faults.
Reporting progress moves tasks and the order to in progress, and 100 percent marks a task completed.
Closing requires root causes, permits and any required meter reading, and the task statuses roll up to the order.
Because status always flows from the work actually done, planners can rely on open requests and orders being genuinely open and still awaiting work.

items.title: Preventive Maintenance Scheduling
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Preventive Maintenance Scheduling

cards.title: Purpose of preventive maintenance scheduling
cards.body:
Preventive scheduling defines when assets should be serviced or inspected, by calendar or by meter reading, and keeps the resulting due dates under control.
Maintenance planners set up schedules, correct individual occurrences and change schedule status.
Planned maintenance happens on time without relying on memory.

cards.title: Schedule, occurrences and status changes
cards.body:
A schedule names the asset, category, work content and one or more time or meter triggers.
Once authorised, it generates dated occurrences as triggers fall due, and maintenance orders are raised against them.
Individual occurrences can be added, re-dated or removed manually, and are marked as manual.
A status change document puts the schedule or its occurrences on hold, cancels or short-closes them, and closing a schedule stops future generation.

items.title: Customer Service Calls
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Customer Service Calls

cards.title: Purpose of the customer service call flow
cards.body:
This flow records each customer request for service, assigns it to a resource, tracks effort and status, and closes it with a solution.
Service desk staff, dispatchers and technicians each own a step, while supervisors watch the live board.
Every customer request is answered, owned and traceable until fixed.

cards.title: Steps from customer call to closure
cards.body:
A service call logs the customer, location, equipment or item, problem and contract coverage.
Calls raised for unregistered items can generate equipment records in bulk, and dispatchers assign resources to many calls at once.
Technicians report time spent on each call, and the monitoring board shows workload by priority.
A status change document moves the call through progress, hold, cancellation or fixed, capturing solution and feedback on closing.

items.title: Service Contracts, Orders and Billing
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing

cards.title: Purpose of service contracts, orders and billing
cards.body:
This flow covers service commitments to customers: contract templates and contracts, service orders for the work, reporting of what was done, and invoicing.
Service managers set up templates, administrators record contracts, coordinators raise and report orders, and billing staff invoice.
Customers are served and billed according to agreed terms.

cards.title: From contract to service order to invoice
cards.body:
A contract setup holds standard terms, and a service contract applies them to a customer's equipment for a period, with pricing, warranty, billing plan and preventive visit triggers.
Contract periods can be extended or shortened, and individual visits corrected.
A maintenance service order is raised from a service call, a contract visit, earlier work or directly, and is amended if scope changes.
Resource time and service reporting record the work, and the customer service invoice bills it.

cards.title: How contract balances and reported work control billing
cards.body:
Service orders raised from a contract visit take the contract's lines, pricing and balances, and cannot exceed the remaining contract quantity or amount.
Amendments cannot reduce quantities below what has been reported or amounts below what has been invoiced, and parts cannot fall below what stores issued.
Service reporting allocates parts from actual issues and sets the order's outcome status.
Invoices against an order cannot exceed what remains to be billed, while contract billing follows the contract's billing plan, and advances are adjusted against the receivable.
Every billed amount can therefore be traced to an agreed contract, an order and reported work.

items.title: Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production

cards.title: Purpose of meter readings and utilisation records
cards.body:
This flow records how equipment and vehicles are used: meter readings, running hours, trips, fuel and material consumed, and shift production.
Operators, drivers and supervisors enter these records daily or per shift.
Usage figures drive meter-based maintenance and cost analysis.

cards.title: How readings stay continuous and trustworthy
cards.body:
Readings are dated, cannot go backwards for running meters, and cannot exceed a daily limit where one is set.
Only one pending reading per object and parameter is allowed, and a later reading blocks an earlier one.
Trip sheets post odometer and hour readings on authorisation, and meter resets record readings before and after so totals stay continuous.
Fuel and consumption entries match material issued from stores with what was actually used per vehicle or component.

items.title: Tyre Management
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Tyre Management

cards.title: Purpose of tyre management
cards.body:
Tyre management follows each tyre through its life: registration, fitment, inspection, removal, repair, retreading and scrapping, with its cost.
Fleet maintenance staff and workshop teams own these steps.
Tyre life, wear and cost are measured per tyre and per life stage.

cards.title: Tyre setup and life cycle steps
cards.body:
Axle and wheel layouts define vehicle positions, and tyre and repair categories define standards and repair types.
Each tyre is registered individually, then fitted, removed or swapped through tyre movements.
Inspections record tread depth, and removed tyres are moved to awaiting repair, retread or scrap through a status change.
Repair requests send tyres out, repair entries record the result, and expense entries add other costs.

cards.title: How tyre status and life stage are controlled
cards.body:
A tyre's status, vehicle and position change only when a movement, status change, repair request or repair entry is authorised, and each change is written to the tyre history.
Each document allows only valid moves; for example, only an available tyre can be installed, and only a removed tyre can be sent for retread.
A completed retread moves the tyre to its next life stage with a new tread depth, while scrapping closes its final stage.
External repairs need proof of return through a service receipt or gate pass before results are accepted.
Because readings are captured at each movement, distance, hours and cost can be compared across tyre makes and categories.

items.title: Incidents and Insurance Claims
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Incidents and Insurance Claims

cards.title: Purpose of incident and insurance handling
cards.body:
This flow records accidents, breakdowns and damage involving equipment or vehicles, reviews them across functions, and raises insurance claims where needed.
Fleet and safety staff enter incidents, each function reviews in turn, and insurance staff file claims.
Each incident is assessed fully and claimed at most once.

cards.title: Incident entry, sequential reviews and claims
cards.body:
An incident records people involved, damaged parts and the reviews required, and must be authorised before review.
Reviews follow a fixed sequence, each function recording its own assessment, and only the technical review can flag an insurance claim.
Review results, such as damage and deduction amounts, are written back to the incident.
An insurance claim ties the incident to a policy document and splits the amount between insurer and company.

items.title: Equipment Master
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Master Data Setup › Equipment Master

cards.title: What the Equipment Master register holds
cards.body:
The Equipment Master maintains every piece of equipment the business owns, hires or services for customers: machines, vehicles, tools and installed components.
Maintenance planners and asset administrators create it when equipment is bought, received, hired in or taken over, and update it as location, custody or parts change.
It gives one coded equipment register on which maintenance, service calls, meter readings and documents are based.

cards.title: Ownership, source documents and serial-based equipment
cards.body:
Equipment can be company-owned or party-owned, and the ownership decides which vendors or customers are offered.
It can be registered directly or from a source document such as a receipt, in which case the reference and the basis are mandatory.
When equipment is based on serial number, the serial number is required and can be copied from the received lot.

cards.title: Codes, hierarchy and inherited defaults
cards.body:
A new equipment receives an automatic code and is saved as authorised.
Choosing the parent equipment copies its category, type, cost center, work center, division and department.
Choosing the equipment type loads that type's default supplemental fields and measurement parameters, which cannot be removed.
Division is mandatory when maintenance runs by division, and a chosen location needs an effective date and fixes the division.
When the company setting is on, a matching component item is created automatically for equipment without an item.

cards.title: Custodian, vehicle, warranty and certificate details
cards.body:
When a custodian is recorded, a contact number and custody date are required, and the custody date cannot precede installation.
Vehicles need a fuel type, can carry a driver with an effective date, and can have a tyre layout.
Where required, the vehicle registration must follow the standard national number pattern.
Warranty lines need a number, date and expiry, certificate lines need a date, and expiry dates can never precede start dates.
Every supplemental field that is listed must have a value.

cards.title: Histories, meter parameters and spare parts on the equipment
cards.body:
Every save writes custodian and location history, and driver history when a driver is chosen, so the equipment's past can always be reconstructed.
Bill of materials lines record spare parts with quantity and life span by time, meter or both; an item appearing more than once is flagged for consumption entry, and these lines also keep a history.
Measurement parameters such as hours carry a date and value, only one hours parameter is allowed, and each also creates a meter reading.
Lines already used by readings are locked, and once equipment is used in a service call or order its item cannot be changed.
These rules keep the register stable enough to support maintenance planning, consumption tracking and service history over the equipment's life.

items.title: Functional Location
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Master Data Setup › Functional Location

cards.title: What a Functional Location represents
cards.body:
A Functional Location is a place in the plant where equipment sits and work is done, such as a building, line, station or bay.
Maintenance planners create it when a plant is set up or extended, or when a place's custody, address or attributes change.
Maintenance teams get one coded list of places to attach equipment and work to.

cards.title: Hierarchy, custody and maintenance attributes of a location
cards.body:
A new location receives an automatic code and is saved as authorised.
Choosing a parent location copies its type, cost center, work center, division and department, and only authorised active locations can be parents.
A custodian requires a contact number and custody date, and every save writes custodian history.
Group templates fill supplementary, measurement, safety and skill details; measurement lines need a value, and lines used by meter readings are locked.

items.title: Permit Master
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Master Data Setup › Permit Master

cards.title: What a Permit Master template defines
cards.body:
The Permit Master maintains reusable work permit templates: the safety conditions, tasks and equipment for a type of hazardous maintenance work.
Maintenance planners set it up when new permit-controlled work is introduced or an existing permit changes.
Isolation, instructions and check lists are applied consistently to every job.

cards.title: Equipment coverage, safety groups and copying permits
cards.body:
Each covered line names an object type and an equipment or location of that type; lines without an object are not kept.
Choosing a safety group replaces the safety instructions with all instructions of that group.
A new permit can be started from an existing one, which is copied without its identity, so saving creates a new template.
Clearance permits later take their instructions and check lists from this template.

items.title: Maintenance Category Task
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Master Data Setup › Maintenance Category Task

cards.title: What a Maintenance Category Task list defines
cards.body:
A Maintenance Category Task list ties one maintenance category to a set of equipment and a list of standard tasks, each with estimated time and priority.
Maintenance planners set it up when they define or revise the standard work for a type of maintenance.
Equipment then carries one agreed task list per category.

cards.title: Task completeness, time entry and one active list per equipment
cards.body:
Every task needs estimated hours and a priority; lines without a task name are ignored.
Estimated hours are entered as hours and minutes, and the minutes cannot exceed 59.
An equipment included here cannot be on any other active task list, which prevents conflicting standards.
Maintenance orders later load these standard tasks for the equipment and category, so planners start from an agreed list instead of building every job from scratch.

items.title: Shutdown Work List
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Master Data Setup › Shutdown Work List

cards.title: What a Shutdown Work List prepares
cards.body:
A Shutdown Work List is a reusable plan of the work done when a group of equipment is shut down: the equipment affected, the planned tasks, and the resources and items each task needs.
Maintenance planners prepare it as the standard shutdown plan.
One agreed plan per equipment is ready to be pulled into a maintenance order.

cards.title: Equipment, tasks, resources and items on the list
cards.body:
A new list receives an automatic code, and an equipment can be on only one work list of the company.
At least one task is required, and each task needs an estimated duration in hours and minutes, with minutes below 60.
Resources need a quantity and a duration, and items need a quantity, with make and grade limited to the item.
Resources and items can be linked to tasks already entered, and new task names are added to the task master.

items.title: Change Equipment Location
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes › Change Equipment Location

cards.title: Why equipment relocation is a controlled document
cards.body:
Change Equipment Location moves one or more pieces of equipment to a new functional location and records who is responsible and who holds custody.
Maintenance planners raise it when equipment moves to another site, building, department or custodian.
After approval the equipment shows the right location and custodian, and every move keeps a history.

cards.title: New location, equipment lines and custodian rules
cards.body:
A new location is required and must differ from the current one; choosing it copies its address and division.
At least one equipment line is required, the same equipment cannot appear twice, and every line needs a relocation reason.
Only authorised, active equipment is offered.
A custodian needs a contact number, and an optional movement period needs a from date that is not after the to date.
Equipment already on another pending location change or replacement cannot be included.

cards.title: What authorisation changes and how child equipment moves
cards.body:
Nothing changes on the equipment until the document is authorised.
Authorisation updates each equipment's location, effective time and division, and writes location and custodian history.
The effective time is the document date plus the time entered, and it must be later than the equipment's latest location entry.
When child parts are to move as well, authorisation relocates the equipment and all of its descendants, so a descendant cannot also be listed separately.
Custodian history is written only when the custodian name or contact actually changes, and an authorised document cannot be edited.
Together these rules keep the equipment hierarchy and its history consistent after every move.

items.title: Change Equipment Owner
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes › Change Equipment Owner

cards.title: Why ownership of customer equipment is changed formally
cards.body:
Change Equipment Owner transfers customer-owned equipment that the company services to a new customer and location.
Service administrators use it when a customer sells or transfers equipment, or when a service contract moves to another customer location.
After approval, service calls, contracts and invoices follow the right customer.

cards.title: Equipment and contract sources and the checks applied
cards.body:
The change can be made for individual equipment or for all equipment of a service contract.
Only authorised, customer-owned equipment with a known customer location is offered, and the new customer location must differ from the old one.
Equipment under an authorised service contract valid today cannot be changed individually, and equipment on another pending change is refused.
The document date cannot precede the last owner change, and on authorisation the equipment's customer location changes, together with the contract's when the contract is the source.

items.title: Change Equipment Driver
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes › Change Equipment Driver

cards.title: Why driver changes are recorded on a vehicle
cards.body:
Change Equipment Driver records which driver, and optionally which shift, is assigned to a vehicle from a given date.
Fleet supervisors use it when a vehicle is handed to a different driver or shift.
The assignment keeps a dated history, so later documents can be traced to the right driver.

cards.title: Which vehicles qualify and how the effective date is checked
cards.body:
Only active automobile equipment of the logged-in company and active drivers and shifts of the company are offered.
The current driver shown is the latest entry for that vehicle.
The effective date defaults to now and must be later than every other driver entry of the vehicle, apart from the initial entry created by the equipment master.
Each save adds a new history entry or corrects the loaded one, and the shift may be left empty.

items.title: Equipment Document Entry
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes › Equipment Document Entry

cards.title: Why equipment documents are recorded
cards.body:
Equipment Document Entry records statutory and commercial documents that belong to a piece of equipment or a functional location, such as road tax receipts, pollution certificates or tracking subscriptions.
Fleet and asset administrators record them when a document is issued, renewed or received.
The business can see which documents exist, who issued them, when they expire and what they cost.

cards.title: Document types, additional details and validity status
cards.body:
Each entry belongs to exactly one equipment or one location, and only active document types of the company are offered.
A document type can carry its own additional details, and those marked mandatory need a value.
If a type does not allow multiple entries, only one entry of that type may exist per equipment or location.
The latest earlier entry is shown for reference, marked expired when its validity date is today or earlier, and the validity date itself is optional.

items.title: Equipment Down Period
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes › Equipment Down Period

cards.title: Why equipment downtime is documented
cards.body:
Equipment Down Period records when and why equipment or functional locations are out of service and for how long.
Maintenance planners raise it for planned shutdowns or other stoppages.
Downtime is documented and linked to the maintenance orders that carry out the work.

cards.title: Down types, estimated and actual dates
cards.body:
A reference object, down type and reason are required; the object decides whether equipment or locations are listed.
For a breakdown the document date cannot precede the start date, while for a shutdown the start date cannot precede the document date and an estimated end date is required.
Actual start and end cannot be earlier than the estimated dates.
Authorisation requires an actual end date, and only authorised down periods are offered to maintenance orders.

cards.title: How actual downtime is derived from maintenance order closings
cards.body:
A down period is planned with estimated dates, but its actual dates come from the maintenance work done.
When authorised maintenance order closings exist for the orders linked to the down period, the earliest closing start and the latest closing end are offered as the actual dates.
A reopened document shows its own saved actual dates only if it is already authorised or has no authorised closing yet.
Because authorisation needs an actual end date, a down period cannot be closed before the work is.
This ties reported downtime to real maintenance effort, giving reliable figures for equipment availability analysis.

items.title: Equipment Replacement Request
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes › Equipment Replacement Request

cards.title: Why equipment replacement is requested formally
cards.body:
An Equipment Replacement Request asks for one or more pieces of equipment to be replaced, with approval.
Maintenance planners raise it when equipment is worn out, damaged or obsolete, often after a maintenance order shows the need.
Replacement decisions are documented and approved before any replacement is carried out.

cards.title: Request sources, equipment scope and overlap checks
cards.body:
A request can be direct or raised from an open maintenance order; an order source requires the order, and the request cannot be dated before it.
For an order source, the order's equipment and all its sub-equipment are offered; otherwise any authorised active equipment of the company.
Requested by and reason are mandatory.
Equipment already on another pending request, on a request still awaiting replacement, or being installed as new equipment elsewhere is refused, and an authorised request is locked.

items.title: Equipment Replacement
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Equipment and Asset Register Changes › Equipment Replacement

cards.title: What an Equipment Replacement records
cards.body:
Equipment Replacement records that one piece of equipment has actually taken the place of another, following an authorised replacement request.
Maintenance planners prepare it once the new equipment is installed.
Equipment locations and custody stay correct, and each replacement is traceable to its request.

cards.title: Request link, old and new equipment and authorisation effects
cards.body:
A request is required, chosen from authorised requests containing the old equipment, and the document date cannot precede it.
The new equipment is required, must differ from the old one and cannot be on another pending replacement or location change.
A responsible person is mandatory, while custodian, location and address details are optional.
On authorisation location history and custodian history are written for both equipment, and the replacement date must be later than their latest location entries.

items.title: Work Log
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Work Log

cards.title: What the maintenance Work Log captures
cards.body:
The Work Log is the maintenance shift diary: logged events, task plan, resources, items, employees involved, comments and costing.
Maintenance supervisors fill it for each shift or day of work.
There is a traceable diary per equipment and shift, plus a ready list of follow-up tasks with the spares they need.

cards.title: Equipment log, daily tasks and follow-up plan
cards.body:
An equipment log needs at least one equipment or location, each with an entry time and description; other log types record daily tasks instead.
Choosing a maintenance category fills the daily tasks with its standard tasks marked completed.
Planned tasks need equipment, execution date and work center, and a child task takes its parent's date.
Resources and items cannot repeat within a task, quantities are required, durations use minutes below 60, and a shift needs a shift in-charge.

items.title: Maintenance Request
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Maintenance Request

cards.title: Why maintenance needs start with a Maintenance Request
cards.body:
A Maintenance Request asks maintenance to look at one equipment or functional location, listing faults or service descriptions with priority and target date.
Operators, supervisors or department users raise it when a fault is noticed, a service is wanted or an earlier request must be repeated.
Every maintenance need is recorded once with an owner, urgency and target date.

cards.title: Request types, dates and duplicate fault prevention
cards.body:
A fault request needs at least one fault and a service request at least one description, and none may repeat.
The occurrence date cannot be after the document date, and the target date cannot be before it.
Only authorised, active equipment or locations are offered, filtered by division where maintenance runs by division.
The same fault cannot be raised again for the same equipment or location while an earlier request for it is still open, and new descriptions are added to the master automatically.

cards.title: Request sources, work log links and approval
cards.body:
A request can be direct or raised from a reference document; a reference requires its number, and the request cannot be dated before it.
For equipment, open work logs can be linked so observations recorded by operators lead straight into a request, and the request cannot be dated before a linked log.
Where multi-level approval is set up, the authorised status cannot be chosen directly, approval levels are saved and the authorisation step runs on save.
Release and authorisation stamp the user and time, and companies can make the shift a warning or a mandatory detail.
Only authorised requests can then be taken into maintenance orders, keeping every job traceable to an approved need.

items.title: Change Maintenance Request Status
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Change Maintenance Request Status

cards.title: Why maintenance request status is changed fault by fault
cards.body:
Change Maintenance Request Status moves the faults of an authorised maintenance request to a new status, such as hold, cancel, in progress, short close, authorised again or completed.
Maintenance supervisors use it when work is paused, started, cancelled or resumed.
The reason and the person behind every change are kept.

cards.title: Allowed next statuses and how the request status follows
cards.body:
Only authorised, on-hold or in-progress requests of the same division are offered, and the document date cannot precede the request date.
The next status depends on the current one; for example, a held fault can only go back to authorised, be cancelled or move to in progress.
At least one fault must be given a status, and changes reach the request only when this document is authorised.
The request then becomes in progress or authorised if any fault still is; otherwise it takes hold, cancel, short close or completed, in that order.

items.title: Maintenance Order
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Maintenance Order

cards.title: What a Maintenance Order plans
cards.body:
A Maintenance Order turns a maintenance need into a planned job on one asset, with tasks, resources, materials, permits and dates.
Maintenance planners raise it when a fault is requested, a scheduled occurrence falls due, an inspection is needed, or a job is started directly.
Each job has one approved plan tied to its source, and work is reported against that plan.

cards.title: Order types and the sources each may use
cards.body:
Orders are preventive, corrective or inspection.
Preventive orders may use any source, corrective orders are direct or from a maintenance request, and inspection orders are direct or from a maintenance schedule.
Tasks, resources, tools and items can be loaded from the schedule, work logs, the shutdown work list or the category's standard tasks.

cards.title: Planned dates, tasks, resources and materials
cards.body:
Estimated start cannot precede the document date, end cannot precede start, and the duration cannot be empty.
The order's window must cover the dates of all tasks and resources.
Except for inspections at least one task is required, each with priority and assignee, and inspection orders need at least one check point.
Resources need quantity and rate type, with hourly amounts calculated from duration, and tools and items need item, description and quantity; duplicate lines are refused.

cards.title: How orders consume requests and schedules and get authorised
cards.body:
Request faults are offered only when the request is authorised, of the same company, division, type and asset, and still authorised or in progress; schedule occurrences follow the same idea.
Unless the order is direct, at least one source line must be selected, and the order cannot be dated before a selected schedule date.
Saving marks referenced faults and occurrences as taken, and recalculates the request status, so each need is consumed by only one order.
A breakdown fault on a request warns the planner if the order is not flagged as a breakdown.
Under multi-level approval the group must be valid and the order cannot be marked authorised directly from entry; release and authorisation stamp the user and time.

items.title: Maintenance Order Amendment
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Maintenance Order Amendment

cards.title: Why authorised maintenance orders are amended
cards.body:
Maintenance Order Amendment revises the plan of an authorised maintenance order in place, keeping its number, date and division.
Planners use it when tasks, dates, resources or material needs change before the order is closed.
The plan stays current while work continues to be reported against it.

cards.title: Eligible orders, protected lines and saving
cards.body:
Only authorised or in-progress orders without a closing document can be amended.
The same header and line rules as the original order apply, and the order date is used for date checks.
Task and resource lines that already have usage or reporting cannot be edited or deleted, nor can tasks with sub-tasks or mandatory permits.
There is no separate approval: every save is recorded as authorised with the saving user and time.

items.title: Clearance Permit
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Clearance Permit

cards.title: Why maintenance work needs a clearance permit
cards.body:
A Clearance Permit grants and documents permission to work on one piece of equipment or one functional location before maintenance starts.
Maintenance and safety officers raise it for maintenance orders that require a permit.
Dangerous work is linked to an approved, dated permit with safety instructions and a check list.

cards.title: Equipment or location, covered orders and permit dates
cards.body:
The permit is raised either for equipment or for a functional location, and only authorised equipment, locations, permits and safety groups are offered.
Choosing the equipment and permit fills permit type, lockout or tagout, eligible orders and the check list.
At least one maintenance order must be selected, and its date cannot be after the document date.
Start date cannot precede the document date and end date cannot precede start date, and closed orders cannot be removed from a saved permit.

cards.title: Where safety instructions come from and how tagout is controlled
cards.body:
Safety instructions come from the permit master when it lists any; otherwise they come from the equipment's or location's safety details, and a chosen safety group takes over.
Instructions are replaced on a change of permit or equipment only while none have been entered yet, so work already done is not lost.
When the lockout type is tagout, the number of tags is mandatory and exactly that many tag lines must be entered, each with tag text.
In division-wise installations equipment, locations and orders are limited to the document's division.
Release and authorisation stamp the user and date, giving a complete safety record for each job.

items.title: Maintenance Reporting
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Maintenance Reporting

cards.title: Why maintenance work is reported shift by shift
cards.body:
Maintenance Reporting records the actual work done, shift by shift, against open maintenance orders or maintenance requests, covering tasks, resources and faults.
Technicians or supervisors enter it at the end of each shift or whenever work is reported.
Actual time, progress and resource use are captured as the work happens.

cards.title: Eligible orders and requests and the entry rules
cards.body:
Open or in-progress orders without a closing, and requests not on hold, cancelled or short-closed, are offered; an order task is offered only while its progress is below 100 percent.
The entry date cannot precede the order or request date, and one report per day and shift collects all entries.
Each task needs a status and, unless held or cancelled, start, end, duration and a progress that only increases and never exceeds 100 percent.
Resources need name, quantity, times and usage, and times cannot overlap earlier reports.

cards.title: How reported progress drives task, order and request status
cards.body:
Reporting 100 percent progress sets the task to completed and locks it.
After each entry the task and order status are recalculated: completed at full progress, in progress once any reporting exists, and open otherwise.
Delay is total duration plus earlier execution time beyond the estimate, and a delay reason can be recorded only while the task is still open.
Faults reported against a request need a description and a root cause, and saving them marks the request fault as taken up.
An order with a closing can no longer be reported on, so the closing document remains the final word on actual work.

items.title: Maintenance Order Closing
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › Maintenance Order Closing

cards.title: What a Maintenance Order Closing records
cards.body:
Maintenance Order Closing records the final outcome of one maintenance order: closing status, actual start and end, duration, delay and reason, and the actual task, resource, fault and check point results.
Planners prepare it when work is completed, cancelled, short-closed, held or still in progress.
The order and its tasks take their final status, and actual times, delays and root causes are on record.

cards.title: Actual times, progress and delay on closing
cards.body:
Only authorised orders not already closed are offered, one closing per order, and no time may be before the order date.
The closing window must cover the earliest and latest task and resource times, and duration is calculated from start and end.
Delay is the duration beyond the estimate, and any delay needs a reason.
A completed status needs progress of 100 percent, progress can never fall below what was already reported, and hold, cancel or short close need a reason.

cards.title: Safeguards before an order can be closed as complete
cards.body:
Every selected fault needs a root cause, and a new root cause typed in is added to the master list.
To complete, each required permit must have a clearance permit, and authorisation is refused when the order needs a meter reading that has not been recorded.
Where configured, shutdown details, root causes and resource names are checked as warnings or hard stops; most of these checks are skipped for a cancelled order.
A warning appears when less material was issued than required, or when issues or service bills exist on a cancelled order.
Task statuses then roll up to the order status, an in-progress closing cannot be authorised, and an authorised closing is locked.

items.title: WBS Task Reporting
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Maintenance Requests, Orders and Closing › WBS Task Reporting

cards.title: What WBS Task Reporting is intended for
cards.body:
WBS Task Reporting is intended to report progress and resource usage against the tasks of a project work breakdown structure, in the same layout as maintenance reporting.
It is meant for project or maintenance work planned as a work breakdown structure.
In its present state it does not store any data, so it delivers no business outcome yet.

cards.title: Current behaviour and limits of WBS Task Reporting
cards.body:
The project list offers the company's authorised projects, and a default project is preselected.
The structure list offers approved revisions that are not the parent of another revision, plus the latest revision of any structure that has tasks, and it is not filtered by project.
No detail is mandatory and no checks run.
Saving, deleting and loading do nothing, so users should continue to report this work through maintenance reporting until the form is completed.

items.title: Maintenance Schedule
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Preventive Maintenance Scheduling › Maintenance Schedule

cards.title: What a Maintenance Schedule plans
cards.body:
A Maintenance Schedule defines recurring or one-off preventive or inspection maintenance for one equipment or functional location, with category, work content and triggers.
Maintenance planners set it up when an asset should be serviced or inspected on a calendar rhythm or on a meter reading such as running hours.
Due maintenance becomes predictable, and orders are raised from dated occurrences.

cards.title: Work content: tasks, resources, tools, items and check points
cards.body:
Only preventive maintenance and inspection can be scheduled.
Preventive schedules need at least one task per trigger, each with priority, assignee and estimated duration; inspection schedules need check points instead of tasks and tools.
Resources and tools need quantity and duration, items need quantity, and the same resource, tool, skill or item cannot repeat for one trigger.
Changing the asset or category reloads its standard tasks and meter parameters, and new task names are added to the task master.

cards.title: Time-based and meter-based trigger setup
cards.body:
A time-based trigger is fixed, on one date, or recurring every so many days, weeks or months, with an end date or a number of occurrences.
Its start date, less any threshold days, cannot precede the document date, and the end date cannot precede the start date.
A meter-based trigger needs a measurement parameter; recurring meter triggers need an interval, and fixed ones need a condition and reading value.
Threshold values cannot exceed the start or interval values, and a readable trigger description is generated automatically.

cards.title: How authorised schedules generate occurrences and orders
cards.body:
Only an authorised schedule generates occurrences; after every save the system evaluates each trigger and adds the due occurrences automatically.
A time trigger fires when its expected date, less threshold days, is reached, and a meter trigger fires when the current reading reaches the expected value.
The order rule decides whether all triggers must fire or any one is enough, and recurring series stop at their end date, count or end value.
With fixed intervals several due points are counted from the planned start; with actual intervals only the next is counted from the previous order, and it waits until that order exists.
The planner can preview time-based occurrences, and when saved as authorised the same schedule can be copied to other assets of the same category and type.

items.title: Maintenance Schedule Occurrence
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Preventive Maintenance Scheduling › Maintenance Schedule Occurrence

cards.title: When a schedule occurrence is maintained manually
cards.body:
Maintenance Schedule Occurrence lets a planner add, correct or remove a single dated occurrence of a trigger on an authorised maintenance schedule.
It is used when the automatically generated series needs a manual addition, a date correction or a removal.
The occurrence list that drives maintenance orders stays correct without re-saving the schedule.

cards.title: Schedule choice, numbering, dates and manual flag
cards.body:
Only authorised or in-progress schedules are offered, and the occurrence belongs to one of that schedule's own triggers.
The occurrence number is automatic: the trigger's highest number plus one.
The date cannot be before the schedule date or before the trigger's previous occurrence.
A warning appears when the expected date or reading differs from the current one, and every save marks the occurrence as manually maintained.

items.title: Maintenance Schedule Change Status
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Preventive Maintenance Scheduling › Maintenance Schedule Change Status

cards.title: Why a maintenance schedule's status is changed formally
cards.body:
Maintenance Schedule Change Status puts a schedule and its pending occurrences on hold, cancels or short-closes them, or releases them back into progress.
Planners use it when equipment is retired, maintenance is postponed, a contract ends or a plan is replaced.
Status changes are traceable and applied consistently to the schedule and its occurrences.

cards.title: Allowed status changes and occurrence lines
cards.body:
Only authorised, held or in-progress schedules without a final change document can be chosen, and the document cannot be dated before the schedule.
The target status depends on the current one; for example, a held schedule can go back to authorised, be cancelled or move to in progress.
Completed occurrences are locked, while every other occurrence needs a status and a reason.
Setting an occurrence to completed only sticks if an order exists for it; otherwise it returns to authorised.

cards.title: Closing a schedule and re-evaluating its status
cards.body:
Changes take effect only when the document is authorised; initial and released documents record the intent without changing anything.
When the schedule itself is to be closed, every open occurrence must have a status, and the user must accept that automatic generation of future occurrences will stop.
When it is not being closed, the schedule status is re-evaluated: it becomes in progress if any order exists and authorised otherwise, and a single-trigger schedule whose series has ended follows its occurrences.
The header status can be copied to lines that already have a status.
Everything is saved together, so the schedule and its occurrences never disagree.

items.title: Service Call
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Customer Service Calls › Service Call

cards.title: What a Service Call records
cards.body:
A Service Call logs a customer's request for service with customer, location, contact, equipment or item, problem, priority, assignee, status and contract coverage.
Service desk staff record it whenever a customer reports a fault or asks for service.
Every request has a traceable number, status history and owner until it is fixed.

cards.title: Customer, equipment and contract coverage on a call
cards.body:
Each call receives an automatic number, and the entry date defaults to now.
Equipment offered is authorised, customer-owned and at the customer location; choosing it fills the item and serial number.
Valid service contracts and invoices still under contract coverage are listed, and when any are listed one must be selected; its end date cannot precede the call.
Earlier calls and service orders for the same equipment or item are shown as service history.

cards.title: Status, assignment history and the service knowledge base
cards.body:
A new call starts as open and can move to in progress, fixed or cancelled; a fixed call locks its details and contract coverage, and a held call can only be changed through a status change document.
Status history is written on creation and whenever the status changes, with the remarks.
The assignee is optional, but each change of assignee adds an assignment history entry.
Feedback values must match their parameter's data type, and notification users cannot repeat.
When the problem and solution are worth keeping, the call can add a knowledge entry, authorised at once and shared across companies, so future calls can reuse the fix.

items.title: Autogenerate Service Call Equipment
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Customer Service Calls › Autogenerate Service Call Equipment

cards.title: Why equipment is generated from service calls
cards.body:
Autogenerate Service Call Equipment creates equipment records in bulk for service calls that were raised against a customer item and serial number but have no equipment attached.
Service coordinators use it when calls exist for items not yet registered as equipment.
Each call then has an equipment record for later service work and contract checks.

cards.title: Which calls are offered and how each row is generated
cards.body:
Calls are listed when they belong to the company, fall in the chosen date range, have an item but no equipment, are not fixed, cancelled or completed, and have no service order.
At least one call must be selected, and each selected row creates one active, authorised machine named after the item and serial number, then links it to the call.
The call date and contract date cannot be earlier than the invoice date.
Each row is generated separately, so a failure is recorded in that row's remarks without stopping the others.

cards.title: Optional contract setup, spare parts and company-specific checks
cards.body:
A service contract setup can be attached while generating, and if one is chosen a contract date is required.
Setups offered must be effective on the invoice date and match the call's item or its sub group.
Spare parts can be stored with the new equipment; each needs a non-zero quantity, and the same alias, item and make cannot repeat.
Companies can switch on extra checks that make serial number, contract setup, spare parts, or invoice number and date mandatory; when none is active those checks do not run.
This lets one bulk action produce equipment that is ready for contract-based service, not just a bare register entry.

items.title: Service Call Resource Allocation
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Customer Service Calls › Service Call Resource Allocation

cards.title: Purpose of bulk resource allocation to service calls
cards.body:
Service Call Resource Allocation lets a dispatcher assign a service resource to many service calls in one pass.
It is used when calls need an owner or must be moved to another resource.
Every call can be traced to a responsible resource, and changes of owner are auditable.

cards.title: Eligible calls, resource choice and assignment history
cards.body:
Open or in-progress calls of the company that have a customer and customer location are listed.
Resources linked to the company are offered, and at least one call must receive a resource.
Calls left blank are skipped, so an owner cannot be cleared here.
The owner is always updated, but a history entry is added only when the resource differs from the latest one, and the history shows who assigned whom and when.

items.title: Service Call Resource Reporting
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Customer Service Calls › Service Call Resource Reporting

cards.title: Why resources report time on service calls
cards.body:
Service Call Resource Reporting lets a service resource record time spent on a service call, with date, duration and remark.
Technicians enter it after working on a call.
Effort per call and per resource is captured for follow-up and costing.

cards.title: Eligible calls, the reporting resource and duration limits
cards.body:
Only open or in-progress calls of the company can be chosen.
The resource is the one linked to the logged-in user, and for a new entry it must be active for the company.
The entry date cannot precede the call date, and only the date is kept.
Duration cannot be zero, cannot exceed 24 hours, and minutes cannot exceed 59; each entry gets an automatic log number.

items.title: Service Call Change Status
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Customer Service Calls › Service Call Change Status

cards.title: Why service call status is changed through a document
cards.body:
Service Call Change Status moves a service call to its next permitted status and records why, with solution, feedback and contract details on closing.
Service coordinators use it when work on a call starts, pauses, is cancelled or is finished.
Only valid moves are allowed, and closing information is captured at completion.

cards.title: Permitted status moves and closing details
cards.body:
From initial or open a call can go to hold, cancel, fixed or in progress; from in progress to hold, cancel or fixed; and from hold back to open.
Calls already fixed are not offered, and the entry date cannot precede the call date.
When completing or fixing, solution and customer feedback are recorded, and a valid contract must be selected where any is listed.
Saving sets the call status and writes history, and the solution can be added to the knowledge base.

items.title: Service Call Monitoring
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Customer Service Calls › Service Call Monitoring

cards.title: Purpose of the Service Call Monitoring board
cards.body:
Service Call Monitoring is a live, read-only board of all service calls of the company, coloured by priority.
Supervisors and coordinators use it whenever they need the current state of calls without editing them.
Urgent, late or unassigned calls stand out without searching call by call.

cards.title: How the board is filled, coloured and refreshed
cards.body:
Each call shows a contact detail built from its contact number and e-mail; calls with neither are not listed.
Rows are coloured by priority using colours each user saves for themselves, and priorities without a colour appear white.
Configured custom details appear as extra information on each call.
The board refreshes automatically when calls change, and nothing on it can be edited, saved or deleted.

items.title: Service Contract Setup
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Service Contract Setup

cards.title: What a Service Contract Setup template provides
cards.body:
Service Contract Setup defines reusable contract templates with standard commercial and service terms, and the rule deciding where each applies.
Service managers maintain it when the company introduces or changes a standard warranty, maintenance or annual maintenance offer.
Contracts start from approved terms instead of being entered from scratch.

cards.title: Where a template applies and default templates
cards.body:
Each rule line uses criteria such as item or sub group, customer or customer group, and country or state, with at most one of each pair and no repeats.
A template marked as default cannot cover items or sub groups already covered by another default template.
Billing details apply only to outbound service, and the billing type decides which dates and values are needed.
Choosing a payment term setting fills the payment details, and at least one term is needed unless billing is periodic.

cards.title: Pricing, preventive triggers and warranty terms in templates
cards.body:
Every service needs at least one pricing line with a rate type; fixed rate and fixed amount exclude each other, and free-of-cost lines need a quantity.
Spare parts and resources carry their own rate types, and rates are locked where the type makes them irrelevant.
Time-based triggers need a schedule type and recurrence with an end condition, and meter-based triggers need a parameter and limits; a trigger used by any line cannot be edited or deleted.
Warranty templates need a condition and either life span or measurement limits, and response and resolution times are entered as hours and minutes.
Because contracts and service call equipment generation start from these templates, errors here repeat across every contract.

items.title: Service Contract
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Service Contract

cards.title: What a Service Contract commits to
cards.body:
A Service Contract fixes what service is promised, for which equipment, for which period and at what price.
Service administrators record it when equipment is sold or installed and a warranty or maintenance commitment begins, or when a vendor commits to service the company's own equipment.
It is the base for service calls, service orders and billing.

cards.title: Contract nature, sources, period and covered services
cards.body:
Outbound contracts can be direct or from a sales invoice or quotation; inbound contracts can be direct or from a purchase invoice, and a reference copies dates, equipment and items.
Start and acceptance dates cannot precede the document date, and the end date cannot precede the start date.
Each covered equipment needs item, serial number, dates and warranty nature, and a template can fill standard terms.
Services need pricing, spare parts need quantity, rate type and rate, resources need rate details, and nothing may repeat for one trigger.

cards.title: Billing plans, warranty terms and preventive visits
cards.body:
Outbound contracts need billing details: bill-to party, payment mode, due days and billing type, plus the dates and value the type demands.
For periodic billing every planned bill carries a value, and the values must add up to the contract value; otherwise at least one payment term is required.
Base and extended warranties need a condition and either a life span with float and base date, or measurement limits, and these set the contract dates.
Triggers schedule preventive visits; each occurrence must fall within the contract period, cannot exceed the number the trigger allows, and follows the contract's status.
Where preventive maintenance is disabled for the company, triggers and occurrences are not used.

items.title: Change Service Contract Period
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Change Service Contract Period

cards.title: When a service contract's end date is changed
cards.body:
Change Service Contract Period moves only the end date of an authorised service contract, together with the end dates of its time-based triggers.
Service administrators use it when a contract is extended, renewed in place or ended early.
The contract stays consistent with its triggers without editing the full contract.

cards.title: Limits on the new end date and trigger dates
cards.body:
The new end date cannot be earlier than today.
It also cannot be earlier than any billing date, service invoice, expected occurrence, service call or service order already recorded on the contract, so existing activity is never left outside the period.
Only time-based triggers are shown and updated, and each trigger end date must fall between the contract start date and the new end date.
The start date can never be after the end date.

items.title: Service Contract Occurrence
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Service Contract Occurrence

cards.title: When contract visits are maintained manually
cards.body:
Service Contract Occurrence adds, changes or deletes one scheduled service visit of an authorised service contract.
Service administrators use it when a visit must be added, re-dated, closed, cancelled or removed outside the generated schedule.
The visit plan is corrected without editing the contract.

cards.title: Contract, trigger and status rules for a visit
cards.body:
Only authorised contracts of the company that have at least one trigger are offered, and the trigger must belong to that contract.
A visit is for an equipment or an item, never both.
The occurrence number is automatic, one higher than the last for that trigger and object.
Only authorised, completed or cancelled can be chosen as status, and every save marks the visit as manually maintained.

items.title: Maintenance Service Order
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Maintenance Service Order

cards.title: What a Maintenance Service Order agrees with a customer
cards.body:
A Maintenance Service Order plans and prices repair or maintenance work on a customer's equipment, with services, parts, resources, expected meter readings, faults and payment terms.
Service coordinators raise it from a service call, a due contract occurrence, follow-up work, or directly.
Work, materials and billing terms are agreed on one document that execution, issue and invoicing all refer to.

cards.title: Sources, customer details and equipment on a service order
cards.body:
A reference is required unless the order is direct, contract occurrences also need the occurrence, and the order cannot be dated before its reference.
Changing the customer reloads its locations and sets the bill-to party; bill-to and due days are mandatory.
Only authorised, active, customer-owned equipment on the reference or at the customer location is offered.
Estimated start and end cannot precede the document date, and at least one payment term with mode and credit days is required.

cards.title: Contract pricing, line limits and postings on service orders
cards.body:
When raised from a contract occurrence, service, parts and resource lines are replaced by the contract's lines with their pricing and balances.
Contract lines cannot exceed their balance quantity or amount, and the rate type decides whether rate or amount is entered.
Order value is the total of service, parts and resource amounts, and a part's quantity cannot fall below what stores already issued against the order.
Proposed accounts are loaded before authorisation, and meter readings on an authorised order are posted to the equipment's reading history.
This keeps contract entitlement, material issued and billing aligned for each customer job.

items.title: Maintenance Service Order Amendment
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Maintenance Service Order Amendment

cards.title: Why authorised service orders are amended
cards.body:
Maintenance Service Order Amendment revises the service, parts and resource lines of an authorised maintenance service order without reopening it.
Service coordinators use it when scope, quantity or price changes, for example when more parts or an extra resource are needed.
The order total stays correct, and work already reported or invoiced cannot be undone.

cards.title: Floors and caps that protect reported and invoiced work
cards.body:
Only authorised or in-progress orders of the company can be amended, and at least one service line must remain.
Quantity cannot fall below what has been reported, amount cannot fall below what has been invoiced, and a part's quantity cannot fall below what stores issued.
Contract lines cannot exceed their balance quantity or amount.
Rate cannot change on contract lines or invoiced lines, and the order value is recalculated from all lines.

items.title: Service Order Resource Reporting Detail
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Service Order Resource Reporting Detail

cards.title: Purpose of resource time reporting on service orders
cards.body:
Service Order Resource Reporting Detail records the time a technician, crew or machine worked against a maintenance service order.
Service coordinators use it when resource work on an authorised or in-progress order needs recording quickly.
Resource time becomes available to the order, its amendments and customer invoicing.

cards.title: Eligible orders, time limits and overlap checks
cards.body:
Only authorised or in-progress orders with planned resources are offered, and only resources planned on that order.
Start, end and total time are required; end cannot precede start, and neither may fall before the document date.
Total time cannot exceed the span between start and end, and quantity cannot exceed the planned quantity.
Times cannot overlap other entries for the same order and resource, and each line is saved as its own record.

items.title: Service Order Reporting
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Service Order Reporting

cards.title: What Service Order Reporting records
cards.body:
Service Order Reporting records what was actually done against an authorised maintenance service order: services, parts, resources, solutions, feedback, faults and equipment part changes.
Service coordinators or technicians prepare it when work starts, progresses, is held or is finished.
Actual work and material are available for invoicing and equipment history.

cards.title: Eligible orders, dates and reported services and resources
cards.body:
Only authorised, unfinished orders of the company and division without another report can be chosen, so each order has at most one report.
The report cannot be dated before the order, and actual start must fall between the order date and the report date, with end not before start.
At least one service is reported, each with quantity no higher than ordered, dates, status and time.
Resources need start, end, time and schedule entries, and their times cannot overlap other reports of the same order.

cards.title: Parts used, equipment part changes and order outcome
cards.body:
Parts consumed are allocated from authorised issues against the order, net of returns; each line cannot exceed what was issued, and the lines must total the item's reported quantity.
For equipment, a replaced part with an old serial number needs a new serial number from stock issued on this report, and saving updates the equipment's parts record.
Fixed and completed statuses are allowed only on an authorised report, and an authorised report cannot stay on hold or in progress.
Saving sets the service order's status to the report's status, and deleting the report returns the order to authorised.
Root causes and solutions can be added to their master lists, so the next technician can reuse them.

items.title: Customer Service Invoice
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Service Contracts, Orders and Billing › Customer Service Invoice

cards.title: What the Customer Service Invoice bills
cards.body:
The Customer Service Invoice bills a customer for service work, with service, parts and resource lines, taxes and advance adjustments.
Service billing staff raise it when work is done, a contract billing date falls due or a direct service sale is made.
Customers are billed from agreed orders, contracts or measured effort, and the receivable is posted in finance.

cards.title: Invoice sources, rate types and balance limits
cards.body:
An invoice can be direct, against a service contract or against a service order; contract and order sources need a reference dated on or before the invoice.
For contracts the basic amount is the contract or schedule value; otherwise it is the total of service, parts and resource amounts.
Each line needs a rate type and a non-zero quantity, and the rate type decides whether rate or amount is entered.
Against a service order, quantity cannot exceed what is still left to invoice, and resource lines need time entries that do not overlap.

cards.title: Advance adjustment, finance vouchers and cash counter entries
cards.body:
Taxes are calculated from the basic amount, and the due date is the document date plus the due days less one.
When the invoice is authorised and has a positive net amount, a journal voucher is built from the basic amount, taxes and line amounts, and it is rebuilt whenever date, division, tax or status changes.
Advances dated on or before the invoice can be adjusted; each adjustment cannot exceed the advance balance, and the total cannot exceed the net amount.
A second voucher moves adjusted advances against the customer receivable.
An authorised cash invoice also creates a cash counter entry, so billing, advances and cash all reconcile with the ledger.

items.title: Meter Reading
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production › Meter Reading

cards.title: Why dated meter readings are recorded
cards.body:
Meter Reading records dated readings of measurement parameters such as running hours, kilometres or fuel for equipment or functional locations.
Operators and supervisors enter it daily, per shift, or when a maintenance order requires a reading.
Maintenance planning then works from validated readings with a running total per parameter.

cards.title: Objects, readings and date order
cards.body:
Readings can be recorded for one equipment or location, or for several objects at once; a single object must be named.
At least one reading must be selected, and hours are entered as hours and minutes below 60.
Neither the previous nor the latest reading date may be after the measurement date.
Where several objects are read together, each utilisation line needs a value and an operator, and the same work cannot repeat on one date.

cards.title: Running totals, daily limits and protection against conflicting readings
cards.body:
For running parameters, an actual reading is the meter value itself, while a difference reading is added to the previous one; the running total grows by the net movement.
An actual running reading can never fall below the previous reading, and where equipment has a daily maximum, the day's movement cannot exceed it.
No other document may hold the same object and parameter at the same time, no other unauthorised reading may be pending, and no later reading may already exist.
Readings before the opening reading are refused, and a missing issued fuel quantity can be a warning or a stop.
These checks keep the reading history continuous, which schedules and fuel analysis depend on.

items.title: Meter Reading Simplified
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production › Meter Reading Simplified

cards.title: Purpose of quick fleet meter entry
cards.body:
Meter Reading Simplified records the daily odometer and hour meter readings of all vehicles or machines at one location in a single pass, with the day's trips or loads and driver.
Site supervisors use it at the end of a shift or day.
Fleet readings are captured quickly while passing the same checks as a full reading.

cards.title: Which equipment is listed and how readings are validated
cards.body:
Equipment placed at the chosen location that has an odometer or hour meter is listed, and a reading can be entered only for a meter the equipment has.
One reading type applies to every line, and hours must have minutes below 60.
Where the equipment has utilisation work, trips or loads and driver are required.
Duplicate, overlapping, pending or out-of-order readings for the same equipment and meter are refused, and totals follow the same calculation as a full meter reading.

items.title: Reset Measurement Parameter
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production › Reset Measurement Parameter

cards.title: Why meter resets are recorded
cards.body:
Reset Measurement Parameter records the moment a meter on equipment or a location is reset, rolled over or replaced, with readings before and after.
Maintenance or fleet staff enter it when an odometer or hour meter goes back to zero or is changed.
Running totals stay continuous, so a reset is not mistaken for a wrong reading.

cards.title: Reset date, readings and pending documents
cards.body:
Only authorised equipment or locations of the company are offered.
At least one parameter must be selected, each with a reading type and readings before and after the reset.
The reset date cannot be after the document date, and no reading may exist after the reset date.
A reset is refused while a trip sheet, meter reading or another reset for the same object is still unauthorised, and an authorised reset posts both readings while keeping the previous total.

items.title: Equipment Running Hours
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production › Equipment Running Hours

cards.title: Why daily equipment running hours are logged
cards.body:
Equipment Running Hours records how many hours each piece of equipment ran on a given day and shift.
Operators or supervisors enter it at the end of each day or shift for the equipment that worked.
The usage figures support maintenance planning and equipment analysis.

cards.title: Running hours entry, shifts and duplicate prevention
cards.body:
All equipment of the company is listed, limited to the document's division where division-wise display is on.
Each selected equipment needs running hours, entered as hours and minutes with minutes no higher than 59, and a default value can be copied in.
The shift is optional and applies to the whole document.
An equipment cannot be reported twice for the same date and shift, and only authorised documents count in equipment reports.

items.title: Trip Sheet
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production › Trip Sheet

cards.title: What a Trip Sheet records about vehicle use
cards.body:
A Trip Sheet records a vehicle's journeys for a day or shift: which driver drove, departure and arrival, locations, and meter readings.
Fleet supervisors or drivers prepare it for every day or shift a vehicle is used.
Vehicle use is traceable by driver and trip, and the vehicle's meters stay current for maintenance planning.

cards.title: Drivers, times and meter readings on each trip
cards.body:
At least one trip with a driver is required, each with departure and arrival date and time, and arrival cannot precede departure.
The first trip's opening odometer must equal the latest recorded reading, each later opening equals the previous closing, and closing must exceed opening.
Hour readings follow the vehicle's hour format, and closing hours cannot be below opening hours.
A shift needs a shift in-charge, and the document cannot be dated before any of its trips.

cards.title: Preventing overlapping trips and posting meter readings
cards.body:
Trips on one sheet cannot overlap each other, even by touching times, and cannot overlap trips on other sheets of the same vehicle.
A sheet cannot be dated earlier than the vehicle's latest other sheet, and a vehicle may have only one unauthorised sheet and no pending meter reading elsewhere.
When the sheet is authorised, each trip posts its closing odometer at the arrival time and its hours, either as a difference or as an actual reading depending on how the vehicle keeps hours.
Those postings pass the same meter history checks as any other reading, so an out-of-sequence trip is refused.
This makes the trip sheet a reliable source of meter readings for usage-based maintenance schedules.

items.title: Fuel Consumption
items.context: Plant Maintenance › Meter Readings, Utilisation and Production › Fuel Consumption

cards.title: Why vehicle fuel consumption is recorded
cards.body:
Fuel Consumption records how much fuel a vehicle used on a given day and where the fuel came from: stock issues, direct stock entries or a fuel station bill.
Fleet staff enter it when a vehicle's fuel use is reported.
Fuel issued to a vehicle is matched with fuel consumed, and fuel bought outside stock is costed to the vehicle.

cards.title: Fuel sources, eligible issues and amount calculation
cards.body:
Only vehicles of the company that have a fuel item are offered.
From stock issues, only issues of the vehicle's fuel item to its cost center with balance left are listed; consumed quantity defaults to that balance and is valued at the issued rate.
Fuel station lines need a driver, a bill date, a quantity and a rate, and direct lines need a date, a quantity and a rate.
No line may be dated after the entry date, and amount is quantity times rate.
